summary: For 5–6-year-olds describing everyday material properties, teach each property as a testable opposite-pair (waterproof/absorbent, transparent/opaque, hard/soft, rough/smooth, stretchy/stiff, bendy/not bendy, shiny/dull) anchored to a hands-on test the child performs — drip water, bend, stretch, hold to a light, feel. The core objective is that a describing word names an OBSERVED behaviour, not something guessed from appearance. Build the vocabulary through naming scaffolds, then move to real (or realistically simulated) tests so children watch a material respond, and apply the words to a design question such as choosing the best material for an umbrella.
misconceptions: Judging a property from appearance instead of testing it — e.g. assuming clear plastic is glass, or that a shiny thing must be metal.
Treating 'transparent' as 'shiny' or muddling see-through with reflective.
Thinking absorbent and waterproof are the same or unrelated, rather than opposite behaviours toward water.
Believing all of one material shares one property (all plastic is hard, all metal is cold/silver), ignoring variety within a material.
Using property words loosely without tying them to an observation, so 'strong', 'hard' and 'stiff' get used interchangeably.

activities.title: Materials test bench: watch the property happen
steps: Set up or use a bench with real materials and simple test tools: a water dropper, a bend/stretch station, and a torch or light source.

Drip the same small amount of water onto a plastic raincoat/sheet and onto a paper towel. Watch the drops bead up and roll off the plastic (waterproof) and soak in and darken the fibres of the towel (absorbent). Say the two property words aloud for what you saw.

Shine the torch beam AT a clear plastic sheet, a piece of tissue, and a wooden block, and look at where the beam lands — do not look back toward the light. Notice the beam passes clearly through the clear sheet (transparent), only some light glows dimly through the tissue (it lets some light through, so it is neither fully transparent nor opaque — sometimes called translucent), and the light is stopped by the wood (opaque). Name what each did.

Try two separate tests: stretch an elastic band (it pulls LONGER when you pull it — stretchy) versus a stiff stick (it does not give — stiff); then bend a bendy strip (it CURVES or folds when you push it — bendy) versus the stiff stick (it will not bend — not bendy). Feel how stretching pulls something longer while bending curves or folds it.
Record each result in a property grid — materials down the side, property words across the top — writing or stamping the word only after you have seen the test.
Finish with the fair-test challenge: 'Which material makes the best umbrella?' Use what you tested to choose and say why.
activities.insight: A property is a behaviour a material shows when you act on it, so a describing word is something you can test and watch happen — not a guess from how the material looks.

activities.title: Name the property: tap-and-reveal vocabulary scaffold
steps: Explore a scene of familiar materials (sponge, window, brick, elastic band, metal spoon, wooden block).
Tap or point to each one to hear/say one or two property words for it — e.g. sponge: 'soft, absorbent'; window: 'hard, transparent'.
Match opposite-pair cards: shiny↔dull, rough↔smooth, waterproof↔absorbent, transparent↔opaque, stretchy↔stiff, bendy↔not bendy.
Play 'guess then check': predict a material's property, then lift the flap (or run the real test) to see the result.
activities.insight: Each property word has a clear opposite and attaches to example materials, giving children the vocabulary they will then verify by testing.

activities.title: Sort and match: check the words are secure
steps: Drag materials into category bins: transparent vs opaque; waterproof vs absorbent.
Match each material to the property word(s) that describe it.
Answer picture-and-audio questions about properties — but only for materials you have already tested.
Separate confusable cases: sort a soft plastic bag (soft but waterproof) and a rough dry sponge (rough but absorbent) so each property is judged on its own.
activities.insight: Property words are secure when a child applies them correctly across varied examples and keeps distinct properties apart.

activities.title: Predict-then-pour: challenging appearance-based judgements
steps: Look at a shiny-looking scrap of satin fabric (checked beforehand to make sure water soaks through it) and a dull, matt plastic bag. Before pouring anything, predict which would keep a small toy dry if you wrapped it, and say WHY.

Pour the same small splash of water over each wrapped toy and watch: with the pre-checked fabric, water soaks through the smart-looking shiny material and the toy gets wet, while water runs off the dull plastic and the toy inside stays dry.
Compare your prediction with what happened and say which property word fits each material now.
Explore counterexamples: feel a soft plastic bag (soft but waterproof), handle a dull grey metal spoon (metal but not shiny), and check something rough that is also absorbent.
activities.insight: Appearance can mislead, and one material comes in many forms — so a property belongs to the tested object, not to how it looks or to the material 'in general'.

checkQuestion: Show a shiny paper towel and a dull grey plastic bag. Say: 'One of these would make a good umbrella and one wouldn't. Which would keep you dry — and how could we FIND OUT if it's really waterproof, instead of just guessing?' Then: 'You said this one is soft — is everything soft also good at soaking up water? Show me something soft that water runs straight off.'
checkAnswer: Chooses the plastic bag (waterproof), uses the property word 'waterproof', and proposes a TEST — pour or drip water and see whether it soaks through — rather than judging by looks. Recognises that 'soft' and 'absorbent' are different properties.
